newsitem.title: MALI: Mali uncovers coup plot, source says.
newsitem.headline: Mali uncovers coup plot, source says.

text.p: Authorities in Mali have uncovered a plot to kill President Alpha Oumar Konare, his prime minister and defence minister and the conspirators have been arrested, a source close to the government said on Monday.
State radio, in brief reference to the affair later, spoke simply of an attempt to destabilise Mali's democratic institutions and said arrests had been made.
The source said one of the plotters, who included an air force officer, other military men and a civilian, was linked to ousted dictator Moussa Troare, who was toppled in 1991.
Konare, a historian, was elected in 1992 as part of a transition towards democracy in the West African state, which is due to hold presidential, legislative and municipal elections early in 1997.

Traore has been in jail since his overthrow. He was sentenced to death in 1993 for murder in connection with the repression of a 1991 democracy protest during which security forces killed more than 100 people, mostly students.
The source said the plot was uncovered overnight and investigations were continuing. Sources close to the armed forces ministry said the plotters were an isolated group.
Court sources said earlier that the constitutional court had blocked a new electoral code, which was passed by parliament but provoked a serious rift with the opposition.
They said the court ruled that 30 of the law's 196 articles, including those relating to the composition of an independent electoral commission, were totally or partly unconstitutional.

Konare's government pushed the new code through parliament on September 27. The opposition, denouncing a lack of dialogue, took part in neither the debate nor the vote and asked the court to review the code in light of its objections.

The opposition, previously fragmented, said the proposed electoral commission, comprising five members each from the ruling party and the opposition plus 10 each for society at large and the public authorities, would not be independent.
It has also described the proposed method of polling -- a mix of proportional representation in some areas and a majority vote in others -- as confusing and unfair.
